content: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), previously referred to as non-insulin-dependent diabetes, obesity-related diabetes, or adult-onset diabetes, is a metabolic disorder primarily defined by insulin resistance, relative insulin deficiency, and elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia). The reduced responsiveness of body tissues to insulin is believed to involve defects in the insulin receptor located on cell membranes. In the early stages of the disease, the primary abnormality is decreased insulin sensitivity, which is often accompanied by elevated insulin levels in the bloodstream (hyperinsulinemia). At this stage, hyperglycemia can often be managed through lifestyle interventions such as regular physical activity, dietary modifications, and medications that enhance insulin sensitivity or reduce hepatic glucose production. However, as the disease progresses, the ability of the pancreas to secrete insulin becomes increasingly impaired, often necessitating insulin therapy. The prevalence of T2DM is rising rapidly in developed countries, and this trend is expected to extend to other regions globally. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has described this increase as an epidemic. Diabetes mellitus has been recognized as a disease since ancient times. In 1812, it was formally identified as a clinical entity in the New England Journal of Medicine and Surgery. By 1889, the pancreas was identified as playing a central role in the disease's pathogenesis. The discovery of insulin in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best marked a pivotal moment in diabetes management, as they successfully reversed diabetes in dogs by administering pancreatic extracts from healthy animals. Type 2 diabetes does not have specific subcategories, but diabetes mellitus as a whole is classified into three main types: type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and gestational diabetes. The pathophysiology of T2DM is primarily driven by the development of insulin resistance. Unlike type 1 diabetes, individuals with T2DM produce sufficient amounts of insulin, but their cells exhibit a diminished response to it. The mechanisms underlying insulin resistance are thought to involve both genetic predisposition and environmental factors. Environmental contributors include diets high in glycemic load, central obesity, advanced age, male sex, low dietary fiber intake, and high consumption of saturated fats. The exact cause of insulin resistance remains unclear, but central obesity, aging, and high-glycemic diets are frequently implicated in its development. T2DM must be distinguished from other conditions that may present with similar symptoms, such as excessive urination (polyuria), excessive thirst (polydipsia), weight loss, or weight gain. Differential diagnoses include other forms of diabetes (e.g., type 1 diabetes, maturity-onset diabetes of the young [MODY]) and endocrine disorders (e.g., hypothyroidism, Cushing's syndrome, Wolfram syndrome, Alström syndrome), as well as drug-induced hyperglycemia (e.g., from glucocorticoids). The prevalence of T2DM has been extensively studied in developed countries, such as the United States, but there is significant variability in data from developing nations, particularly in rural areas with limited healthcare access. Globally, it is estimated that approximately 50% of adults with diabetes remain undiagnosed. In the United States, certain ethnic groups, including African Americans, Mexican Americans, American Indians, and non-Hispanic Blacks, are at higher risk of developing T2DM compared to non-Hispanic Whites. The disease is more common in individuals over the age of 65, although there is a concerning rise in childhood-onset T2DM. In 2011, an estimated 335 million people worldwide had T2DM, and this number is projected to exceed 500 million by 2050. The prevalence rates correspond to approximately 5,000 cases per 100,000 people in 2011, increasing to 7,500 per 100,000 by 2050. T2DM is more common in men than women and is more prevalent in lowto middle-income countries compared to high-income nations. It is considered a global epidemic, closely linked to rapid urbanization. Risk factors for T2DM include a family history of diabetes, certain ethnic backgrounds, obesity, smoking, physical inactivity, poor dietary habits, the use of certain medications (e.g., glucocorticoids), and medical conditions that promote weight gain or inactivity. Screening for diabetes is recommended for individuals at various life stages and for those with specific risk factors. The same tests used for diagnosis are employed in screening. Early detection and treatment can help prevent complications and improve clinical outcomes. If left untreated, T2DM can lead to acute complications such as hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) and, in rare cases, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Chronic complications include microvascular damage (e.g., retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular complications (e.g., cardiovascular disease, stroke). Early diagnosis and timely management of these complications can improve prognosis and reduce long-term morbidity and mortality. A thorough medical history is essential for individuals presenting with symptoms of diabetes. Classic symptoms include weight loss, excessive hunger (polyphagia), excessive thirst (polydipsia), and excessive urination (polyuria). Less common symptoms may include visual disturbances, tingling or numbness in the extremities, fatigue, and skin changes. Physical examination findings are often normal in T2DM patients unless complications have developed. Common findings may include pigmented skin patches and acanthosis nigricans. Laboratory tests are critical for diagnosing T2DM. Diagnosis can be made using plasma glucose criteria, including fasting plasma glucose (FPG), the 2-hour plasma glucose (2-h PG) value following a 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or glycated hemoglobin (A1C) levels. All of these tests are equally valid for diagnosis. Lifestyle modification is the cornerstone of T2DM management and includes diabetes self-management education (DSME), diabetes self-management support (DSMS), nutritional therapy, regular physical activity, smoking cessation counseling, and psychosocial care. The goals of DSME and DSMS are to empower patients to make informed decisions, adopt self-care behaviors, solve problems, and actively collaborate with healthcare providers to improve clinical outcomes, health status, and quality of life in a cost-effective manner. The primary objectives of medical therapy are to alleviate hyperglycemic symptoms, prevent long-term complications, and enhance the patient’s quality of life. Initial treatment typically involves lifestyle changes and weight loss, particularly in obese individuals. Metformin is the first-line pharmacologic agent unless contraindicated. If glycemic targets are not achieved, a second medication is added to metformin. The choice of additional therapy depends on the patient’s clinical condition and comorbidities. For patients with an A1C level greater than 9%, dual oral therapy is initiated. For those with an A1C level exceeding 10%, blood glucose levels above 300 mg/dL, or significant symptoms, combination therapy with insulin is considered. In select cases, surgical interventions such as pancreas or islet cell transplantation may be considered for patients with chronic diabetes who experience frequent metabolic complications, are intolerant to exogenous insulin, or have failed insulin therapy. Primary prevention of T2DM focuses on lifestyle modifications, including weight loss and increased physical activity. Studies have shown that a 7% reduction in body weight over six months in obese individuals can effectively prevent diabetes. Secondary prevention strategies aim to reduce macrovascular complications.
